summary: Japan is an island nation in East Asia made up of islands including Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu. Blending long-standing tradition with modern technology, it is one of the world's major economies.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Although many Japanese visit shrines and hold funerals at temples, they do not consider themselves to "believe" in any religion, because State Shinto was abolished after the Second World War, and the 1995 Aum Shinrikyo gas attack also made people wary of organized religion. Religion in Japan is mostly expressed through custom and seasonal events rather than personal doctrinal identification, so those who call themselves non-religious are the largest group in polls.

ranking.name: Buddhism
ranking.description: Buddhism arrived in the 6th century via Baekje; in the Nara period Emperor Shomu built Todai-ji, and in the Kamakura period the Pure Land, True Pure Land, Zen and Nichiren schools arose, spreading Buddhism to commoners. The Edo shogunate used the "temple certification system" (terauke) to require every household to register as parishioners of a Buddhist temple to prove they were not Christians; this system tied Buddhism closely to family funerals and ancestor veneration, which continues to this day.

ranking.name: Shinto and new religions
ranking.description: Shinto is Japan's indigenous faith, worshiping numerous kami such as Amaterasu Omikami. There are about 80,000 shrines nationwide, and New Year visits and rites such as Shichi-Go-San are held at shrines, but many people do not regard it as a "religion". The new religions are groups that have arisen since the late 19th century, such as Tenrikyo and Soka Gakkai; among them Soka Gakkai has supported the Komeito party in politics and holds some political influence.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: In 1549 the Jesuit Francis Xavier arrived in Kagoshima to preach, and by the late 16th century Kyushu had at one point several hundred thousand believers, but Toyotomi Hideyoshi and then the Tokugawa shogunate successively banned Christianity, and after the Shimabara Rebellion of 1637 believers were forced underground as "hidden Christians". The Meiji government lifted the ban in 1873, but Christianity never spread widely, with believers only about 1–2 percent, though Christian-style weddings and Christmas have become part of popular culture.

religion.background: Japan originally had Shinto, a faith that worships nature and ancestral spirits. In 538 (some say 552) Buddhism arrived via Baekje on the Korean Peninsula and was vigorously promoted by members of the imperial family such as Prince Shotoku, and thereafter the kami and the buddhas were long fused. In 1549 the Jesuit Francis Xavier introduced Catholicism, but from 1612 the Tokugawa shogunate banned Christianity and used the temple certification system to require everyone to register at a Buddhist temple, so Buddhism became deeply embedded in the funeral rites of every household. In 1868 the Meiji government separated Shinto and Buddhism and promoted State Shinto; after the Second World War, in 1946, the emperor issued the Humanity Declaration (Ningen-sengen), and the constitution established the separation of religion and state. Today most Japanese visit shrines at New Year and hold Buddhist funerals, yet consider themselves "non-religious"; belief is more like a custom of daily life.

language.official: Japanese law does not specify an official language; Japanese is the de facto national language.

ranking.name: Japanese
ranking.description: Japan is a highly linguistically homogeneous country that developed as an island nation from ancient times. In the Meiji period a standard language was established based on the Tokyo dialect and spread nationwide through schools, the military and radio, which began broadcasting in 1925, so regional dialects gradually gave way to the standard language. The Ainu language nearly disappeared under the colonization and assimilation policies in Hokkaido, and the Ryukyuan languages of Okinawa also declined because of kominka education.

ranking.name: Chinese
ranking.description: The history of Chinese in Japan can be traced back to the Tojin-yashiki (Chinese quarter) of Nagasaki in the Edo period, and after the ports opened in the Meiji era, Chinatowns also formed in Yokohama and Kobe. From the 1980s Japan opened to international students and technical trainees, and Chinese immigration increased greatly; Chinese are now Japan's largest foreign group, so Chinese has become one of the most common foreign mother tongues in Japan.

ranking.name: Korean
ranking.description: Korean residents of Japan (Zainichi Koreans) mainly descend from Koreans who came to Japan for economic reasons or wartime mobilization during Japan's rule over Korea from 1910 to 1945, and their descendants, concentrated in places such as Tsuruhashi in Osaka. Many of the third and fourth generations now have Japanese as their mother tongue, and Korean speakers in recent years are mostly new immigrants and international students.

language.history: The origin of Japanese remains unsettled, and it belongs to the Japonic family together with the Ryukyuan languages. Japan originally had no writing; around the 5th–6th centuries Chinese characters were introduced via the Korean Peninsula, and in the 8th century the Kojiki and the Man'yoshu recorded the sounds of Japanese in Chinese characters (man'yogana), from which hiragana and katakana were later simplified around the 9th century. In the Heian period court women wrote works such as The Tale of Genji in hiragana, laying the foundation of the Japanese literary tradition. After the Meiji Restoration the government promoted "genbun itchi" (unifying spoken and written language) and a standard language based on the Yamanote dialect of Tokyo, spread nationwide through compulsory education and radio; after the Second World War, in 1946, the Tōyō kanji list was promulgated, simplifying the writing system.

ranking.name: Sushi
ranking.description: Vinegared rice paired with raw fish, seafood or vegetables, in common forms such as nigiri and maki. Freshness of the fish and the vinegar flavor and temperature of the rice are prized, and it is a representative of Japanese cuisine.
ranking.history: Sushi originates in nare-zushi, the fermentation of fish together with rice for preservation in Southeast Asia and China; it had reached Japan by the Nara period, and funa-zushi from Shiga still preserves this ancient form. In the Edo period people began to season with rice vinegar, shortening the preparation time, and around the 1820s nigiri sushi, shaped and eaten on the spot, appeared in Edo (today's Tokyo), sold at roadside stalls as fast food of the day. After the Second World War refrigeration spread and raw-fish sushi moved upmarket; in 1958 conveyor-belt sushi appeared in Osaka, and in the 1970s–80s sushi swept the world along with Japan's economic rise.

ranking.name: Ramen
ranking.description: Wheat noodles in a broth of pork bones, chicken bones, soy sauce or miso, topped with chashu, menma (bamboo shoots), scallions and other toppings. The broth and noodle types vary by region, and it is one of Japan's most popular national foods.
ranking.history: Ramen originates in Chinese noodle soup; after the ports opened in the Meiji era, the Chinatowns of Yokohama and elsewhere began selling "Shina soba" or "Nankin soba", and Rairaiken in Asakusa, Tokyo, in 1910 is considered the first ramen shop run by Japanese. After the Second World War, large quantities of American-aid wheat flour made ramen stalls spread rapidly during the food shortage; in 1958 Momofuku Ando of Nissin Foods invented instant ramen, bringing ramen into every household. Today there are dozens of regional ramen across Japan, such as Sapporo miso and Hakata tonkotsu.

ranking.name: Tempura
ranking.description: Seafood or vegetables are coated in a thin batter made with cold water and deep-fried, giving a crisp coating, and eaten dipped in tentsuyu sauce or salt. Light batter and eating it freshly fried are prized, and it is often served with grated daikon.
ranking.history: In the 16th century Portuguese missionaries and merchants came to Nagasaki and brought the cooking method of frying; the word "tempura" is generally thought to come from the Portuguese têmporas, the Ember Days when Catholics abstain from meat and eat fried fish in the four seasonal fasts. In the Edo period, as the price of oil fell, tempura became a commoner's snack of Edo street vendors, made with fresh fish and shrimp from Tokyo Bay; only after the Meiji era did it develop into a high-class ryotei dish.

ranking.name: Miso soup
ranking.description: A soup in which miso is dissolved into a dashi stock made from kelp or bonito flakes, with ingredients such as tofu, wakame and scallions. It appears at almost every meal and, with white rice and side dishes, forms the basic meal of the Japanese household.
ranking.history: The prototype of miso may have come from China or the Korean Peninsula in the Asuka and Nara periods, at first as a seasoning of the nobility. In the Kamakura period Zen temples dissolved miso in hot water to drink, forming miso soup, and developed the simple meal form of "ichiju issai" (one soup, one dish). In the Sengoku period miso became military rations because it keeps for a long time, and in the Edo period it spread to commoners, with regions developing rice miso, barley miso, soybean miso and others; today it remains an indispensable soup on the Japanese daily table.

ranking.name: Okonomiyaki
ranking.description: Batter is mixed with cabbage, meat or seafood and pan-fried into a pancake on an iron griddle, brushed with thick sauce and mayonnaise, and sprinkled with bonito flakes and aonori.
ranking.history: The predecessor of okonomiyaki can be traced to the Taisho-period "issen yoshoku" (one-sen Western food), a children's snack of batter fried with a small amount of toppings such as scallions. After the Second World War, with food scarce, people added plenty of cabbage to the batter to make it more filling, and okonomiyaki quickly became popular in Kansai and Hiroshima. "Okonomi" means "as you like", meaning toppings can be added freely; the Osaka style mixes the ingredients together before frying, while the Hiroshima style layers them and adds noodles, and the two places often compete over which is "authentic".
